20.0.0.en: The people were about to enter into battles with the inhabitants of the Promised Land. Those nations possessed a great deal of military equipment, including horses and chariots, while the army of Israel had none of it; they were infantry only. Therefore the Lord commanded them not to fear the strength of the enemies and their equipment, and reminded them that, just as He had been with them and brought them out of the land of Egypt, delivering them from Pharaoh and his army, so He is still with them, fighting for them in their holy wars.

20.1.0.en: Before entering any war, the people had to listen to their priests, to whom the Lord had entrusted a role in preparing for war. For example, the priest was to encourage the people, remind them of the Lord's promises, bless them, pray to God to give them victory, and offer burnt offerings and peace offerings (1 Sam 13:9).

20.2.0.en: The priest says to them: you are now ready for war against your enemies, so be strong and take courage, do not be fainthearted before the enemy, and let no doubt of victory trouble your hearts. However well armed the enemy may be, do not fear them and do not dread their violence.

20.3.0.en: And he tells them the reason for this confidence and strong faith in victory over the enemy: that the Lord goes before them and fights for them, and it is He who will give them the victory.

20.3.1.en: Do not fear the wars of the devil or the threats of any man, for God is with you. Hold fast to Him and ask for the intercession of the saints, and you will be victorious in all your wars.

20.4.s.en: (2) Exemption of certain groups from war

20.4.0.en: The officers: the leaders of the people.

20.4.1.en: The following groups are exempted from war:

20.4.2.en: 1- One who has built a house and has not dedicated it and rejoiced in it, so that he does not enter the war sorrowful and fight without strength.

20.4.3.en: 2- One who has planted a vineyard and has not eaten of its fruit.

20.4.4.en: 3- One who has betrothed a wife and has not married her and rejoiced in her.

20.4.6.en: It is noted that these exemptions were for the following reasons:

20.4.7.en: 1- The human feelings of one who has acquired something new, or is bound in an emotional relationship, or is overcome by fear.

20.4.8.en: 2- Presenting men who are full of zeal and strength, not sorrowful or preoccupied with material matters, or fighting against fear, which would hinder them from victory.

20.4.9.en: 3- If the number of men is small, the rest believe that victory comes through God and not through numbers, as happened with Gideon (Judg 7:7).

20.5.0.en: After those exempted from war are sent away, the officers are appointed as leaders of the soldiers to lead them in the war.

20.5.1.en: May you be considerate of people's feelings when you deal with them, especially when you give them responsibilities to carry out, and support them with your encouragement, so that you may reap good results from their work.

20.6.0.en: In this verse, and up to (v. 15), he speaks of the case of fighting against a distant city, while in (vv. 16-18) he speaks of the case of fighting against a city in the Promised Land. In the first case, the first thing to be done is to summon that city to peace, that is, to invite it to make a treaty. God commands this because, if these distant cities were left alone, they might fight against them, so it is necessary to subdue them and put their men to forced labor.

20.7.0.en: If the city responds to the call to peace, the sentence of annihilation is not applied to its inhabitants, but they become servants of Israel, and Israel puts them to work in farming and building. Many of them converted to Judaism and gained rights like the rest of the Jews because of the good treatment the Jews showed them.

20.8.0.en: But if that city refuses the offer of peace and prepares for war against you, then you must lay siege to it.

20.9.0.en: When God gives you victory over it, kill all its males with the sword, but the women, the children, the animals, and the rest of the spoil found in the city, whether money or possessions, you shall take for yourselves. This is as happened in the killing of the Midianites in the days of Moses (Num 31:25-30), and of Ai in the days of Joshua (Josh 8:2). The spoil is considered a reward that the Lord appointed for them as payment for their participation in holy wars, which are the wars of the Lord.

20.10.0.en: The Lord laid down this conduct for them in the case of war with a distant nation, not one of the Canaanite nations dwelling in the Promised Land, because the distant cities, by reason of their distance, posed no danger to their spiritual life.

20.10.1.en: Give an opportunity for understanding with those around you, so that you may save much effort and reach your goals quickly. Do not rush into thinking evil of others and so sin against them and against God.

20.11.s.en: (4) The annihilation of the pagans and of the trees

20.11.0.en: As for the peoples of the land, under their various names, who dwell in the cities within the bounds of the Promised Land, they are to be placed under the ban completely, that is, all their inhabitants are to be destroyed according to the Lord's command, in order to be rid of idol worship and evil lusts, so that the people of God may live in purity. The reason here is the destruction of evil, not hatred, whereas in the New Testament, after faith has been established, God requires us to love our enemies.

20.12.0.en: Allowing these peoples to remain carried the danger of their influencing the people of Israel, enticing them to their idolatrous worship of their gods, with the defilements contained in the rituals of those cults and the rebellion against the true God that they involve, so that the people would sin against the Lord.

20.13.0.en: While you are besieging a certain city, before you enter that city and take it, if you find trees that bear edible fruit, do not cut them down, because they are needed for your food, and cutting them down would be the loss of something important and necessary for human life. Moreover, these trees pose no danger to you: they are not men who could resist you in the siege, nor is there fear that they would turn back with a new war against you, nor will they harm you spiritually.

20.14.0.en: But the other, unfruitful trees you may cut down and use their wood for the siegeworks necessary for besieging cities, until their people surrender to you.

20.14.1.en: Cut off every cause of evil, however dear it may be in your eyes, so that you may live purely and give the devil no opportunity to fight you through it.

20.14.2.en: The unknown murderer, the marriage of the captive woman, the treatment of sons, and the crucified

21.0.0.en: Murder is one of the gravest sins forbidden by the Ten Commandments (Ex 20:12), and it carries a severe penalty in the case of deliberate murder (ch. 19). But if the body of a slain man is found in the field and it is not known who killed him, what are they to do? This is what he will explain in the following verses.

21.1.0.en: A group of the elders and judges of the people is chosen to measure the distance from the place where the body was found to the surrounding cities, in order to determine the city nearest to the scene, since it is most likely that the murderer was from that city.

21.2.0.en: Yoke: the piece of wood placed on the neck of the animal that pulls the plow or turns the waterwheel.

21.2.1.en: After the nearest city is determined, it becomes the duty of its elders to bring a heifer of the herd that has not yet been used in any farm work and has not been placed under a yoke.

21.2.2.en: In the rest of the ritual this heifer will be slaughtered, as a symbolic carrying out of the death penalty that ought to be carried out on the unknown murderer. Therefore the condition that it had never been used before points to the person of the murderer, who is of no use to his society and his people, and from whom no good work comes.

21.3.0.en: They take the heifer and bring it to a valley with a flowing stream of water, which has not been plowed or sown by anyone, and they slaughter it there. The valley that has not been plowed or sown by anyone also points to the murderer, from whom nothing useful is expected, and the flowing stream of water points to the washing away of sin and forgiveness for the people of the city.

21.4.0.en: The priests, the sons of Levi, must be present to supervise the ritual described, because the Lord has chosen them as stewards of the Law and its application, and to bless the people, and according to what they judge, every case, dispute, or disagreement between members of the people is decided, as well as any assault by one person on another, such as beating or killing.

21.5.0.en: Washing the hands is an act that symbolizes a declaration of the innocence from guilt of the one who washes his hands in a particular situation. Something like this was done by Pontius Pilate when he pronounced the sentence of the crucifixion of Christ, and it is done by the priest in the Divine Liturgy to declare his innocence of responsibility for whoever approaches Communion unworthily. This symbolic act is also performed in the setting out of this ritual, since the elders of the nearest city, after slaughtering the heifer, must wash their hands over it as a sign of their innocence of the blood of the slain man.

21.6.0.en: The washing of the hands is accompanied by their declaration in a loud voice that they have not come to know the offender and did not see the murder as it was happening.

21.7.0.en: Then they turn in prayer to God, asking forgiveness and entreating Him not to lay upon them the responsibility for the blood of the one who was killed, remembering that they are the people whom the Lord acquired and delivered from the bondage of Pharaoh. When this ritual is followed in full, the Lord answers the prayer of the elders and forgives His people, and the charge of shedding the blood of the slain man is not laid upon the people of the city.

21.8.0.en: What is right in the eyes of the Lord: carrying out the ritual, as well as God's commandments.

21.8.1.en: If you carry out what the Lord commanded of ritual for this event, and your conduct is according to the Lord's commandments and in keeping with His Law, the responsibility for shedding this blood will not fall on you.

21.8.2.en: If you see anything wrong, do not be hasty in judging and thinking evil of others, but ask God to forgive the one who erred and to help him, or to help the one to whom harm has happened.

21.9.s.en: (2) The marriage of the captive woman

21.9.0.en: Verses (10:14) speak of the conduct toward the women who are taken captive in one of the wars. The Lord commanded them to treat prisoners and captives well, and these are from the peoples whom God did not command to be placed under the ban, that is, to have everyone in them killed, as with the Canaanite peoples.

21.10.0.en: If one of the victorious warriors, or one of the people, sees a woman among the captives and is pleased with her beauty, so that his heart is attached to her and he wants to marry her, he must apply the Law that the Lord dictates to him in the following verses.

21.11.0.en: He must take her to his house, shave her head, and trim her nails. These two customs were among the signs of grief and mourning, and this means giving her an opportunity to grieve for those she has been parted from, family, relatives, and loved ones.

21.12.0.en: He changes her clothes: instead of the clothes she was accustomed to wear, which may have had a special appearance connected with idol worship, he gives her clothes suitable for the people of God, and she remains in his house mourning her father and mother for a full month, and after that he marries her. Her remaining in his house a month before the marriage is for the following reasons:

21.12.1.en: 1- An opportunity for her feelings to calm because of her deprivation of her family and her country; it is a kind of gentleness and compassion and respect for her feelings.

21.12.2.en: 2- An opportunity for her to learn faith in God and His worship.

21.12.3.en: 3- So that she may forget idol worship and all the customs connected with it.

21.12.4.en: 4- So that the new husband may be certain of his feelings toward her, for it is like a period of engagement.

21.13.0.en: Enslave her: from servitude, that is, to make her a slave girl.

21.13.1.en: If it happens that after a period of marriage the husband no longer wishes to continue living with her, the Lord has set down a text in His Law to protect her, and does not allow her to be mistreated or exploited. He must set her free, and the Law does not permit him to sell her as a slave girl, because she had been his lawful wife in fact, so it is not right for him to take her as a slave girl. Releasing her as a free woman is compensation to her for his change of mind about remaining with her as a wife, and it is enough that he has grieved and humiliated her by divorcing her.

21.13.2.en: May you be considerate of the feelings of those around you, especially those to whom you have done wrong; you must apologize to them, and even compensate them for any harm that befell them because of you.

21.14.0.en: The following text protects the rights of the firstborn son of a man married to more than one wife, and it addresses the question of discrimination among children. Suppose a man is married to two women and prefers one to the other, and he has children by both of them, but the firstborn son is from the wife whom he loves less than the other.

21.15.0.en: When he divides his property among them or writes his will, it is not lawful for him to deprive the firstborn son of the hated wife of the right of the firstborn and give it to another son among the sons of the beloved wife. And if Jacob honored Joseph and made him the firstborn (Gen 48:22), it was not because he was the son of Rachel the beloved, but for his faithfulness, obedience, and service to his father and brothers more than the rest of his sons, whereas Reuben the firstborn lost his birthright because he lay with his father's wife (Gen 35:22).

21.16.0.en: Rather, he must understand and acknowledge that the son of the wife who is less favored by him is the firstborn, and he must give him the right of the firstborn, a double portion of his property, because he is the first fruit of his strength, whom he begot in the prime of his power. A double portion: that is, twice the share of any of his brothers.

21.17.1.en: The commandment here speaks of the disobedient son who does not listen to the voice of his father or the voice of his mother, while they try to discipline him and correct his conduct, but he refuses advice and does not submit to them.

21.18.0.en: The gate of his place: the gate of the city.

21.18.1.en: The parents must then take him to the elders of the city who are responsible for examining matters that threaten order and the family, to where they usually gather at the gate of the city, which is the place designated for holding trials.

21.19.0.en: The parents complain to the judges about their son, that he is a disobedient son who defies them, does not obey them, and does not listen to their advice, and in addition to that he is a spendthrift and a drunkard; that is, they state his evil deeds, which are considered a danger to society and the family. This of course does not happen with any parents except when they are unable to correct the behavior of their son.

21.20.0.en: The judgment of the Law on such a disobedient son was stoning to death, and thus the doers of evil are removed from among the holy people, and others hear of this sentence, so that matters are set right and what is crooked is straightened, through the sons' fear that their disobedience might bring them to such an end.

21.20.1.en: If stubbornness toward parents deserves the sentence of death, what then would be the sentence for stubbornness toward God Himself? Many among us resist the Lord's call to them and linger in returning to the bosom of the Church, our mother. Let us take heed before it is too late and we lose our worthiness as sons and heirs of the Kingdom.

21.21.0.en: In the case of carrying out the death sentence on any person and killing him, and afterward hanging his body on a tree, the following must be observed, as stated in the next verse.

21.21.1.en: It is noted that execution among the Jews was not by crucifixion as with the Romans, but he was first put to death in some way, such as stoning, and then his body was hanged on a tree, that is, crucified, in order to publicize his sin so that people would fear and not sin as he did.

21.22.0.en: The Law requires that he not be left hanging on the wood of the cross until the next day, but that he must be taken down from the cross and buried on the same day (which was what was done in the crucifixion of our Lord Jesus Christ). The wisdom in this is that man is created in the image of God, so the exposure of him must not be prolonged; the exposure of his sin has been sufficient on the same day. And the body's remaining hanging means the continued proclamation of the crime connected with it, which made the one hanged accursed of God, that is, under His wrath, because he broke His Law and dared the heinous deed for which he deserved this sentence. Also, the Law's insistence on the necessity of burying the body on the same day is because God does not want our fear of our sins to dominate our thinking for long, as long as the body remains hanging, rebuking us; rather, He asks us to repent of them and to occupy our thoughts with God as the forgiver of sins and not as our judge; in addition, bodies that are not buried spread diseases.

21.22.1.en: That you defile not your land which the Lord your God gives you for an inheritance: the bodies of the slain were considered an uncleanness that defiled the land, so they had to be buried quickly.

21.22.2.en: How great is God's love for us in sending His beloved Son to redeem us from the curse of the Law, being made a curse for us, for it is written, "Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree" (Gal 3:13). He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness. Let us therefore come with confidence to the throne of grace, offering true repentance, assured of its acceptance, believing in Him who redeemed us and opened for us the way to the Kingdom, meditating on the saying of the Apostle Paul: "Every transgression and disobedience received a just recompence of reward; how shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation" (Heb 2:2, 3). Compassion, mixing, and adultery
